subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: pre-departure checklist and task decomposition [Action]
passage: I'm Minakshi, and a checklist saved me. Two weeks before leaving for college in another city, my father Chetan and I sat with a fresh notebook and wrote everything in groups: identity papers, admission letters, bank access, medicines, clothes, phone contacts. Each evening we ticked off one group. On day three we photocopied my papers and put the originals in a folder. On day six I set up online banking with him beside me and wrote the helpline number on a card. He kept saying, “Clothes come last, they're the easy part.” So the night before my train, I packed only what was left: clothes, a lamp, chargers. My bag was ready, and I slept. Looking back, breaking one huge word, moving, into small ticks made it feel possible.

qa.q: Which groups of things did Minakshi and Chetan write in the notebook?
qa.a: They wrote identity papers, admission letters, bank access, medicines, clothes and phone contacts.

qa.q: How did the list change Minakshi's feeling about moving?
qa.a: Minakshi felt calmer and more capable, since breaking moving into small ticks made it feel possible, and Minakshi slept the night before leaving.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if some papers turned out to be missing at the last minute?
qa.a: Minakshi could ask the college office which originals are needed and how to get copies, because a checklist ticked early shows gaps before departure day.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt during the two weeks of ticking off groups?
qa.a: Chetan probably felt reassured, since working on each group with Minakshi let him see the move was prepared and made it easier to let go.

grounding: A teen lists documents, papers, bank access, medicines, clothes and contacts, ticks them off over two weeks with a parent and packs essentials last.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: researching housing and neighbourhood safety [Action]
passage: Sit, Trisha, before your father pays anyone a rupee. Your Shalini Bua has a story about that. When I was seventeen and heading to college in Nagpur, Papa and I lined up one hostel and two paying-guest rooms. We read what earlier residents had written, but I also phoned three seniors and asked plain things: how long is the commute, is the food edible, is it safe to walk back after evening class? Then Papa took a day off from his shop and we saw all three in person before anyone handed over a deposit. The cheapest room had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight. I picked the hostel near the bus stop. It cost a little more, but I slept easily there for three years.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cheapest room?
qa.a: It had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight.

qa.q: Why did Shalini phone seniors and ask such plain questions?
qa.a: She was cautious and wanted honest answers about the commute, the food and safety before any money changed hands.

qa.q: What could someone do if they cannot visit the places in person?
qa.a: They could take a video tour with a parent and talk to current residents, since that lets them see the place and hear honest experiences before paying.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen the extra visits?
qa.a: Papa may have found them tiring, but Papa probably felt reassured to see the places in person, since Shalini's safety and the deposit were both at stake.

grounding: With a parent, a student compares hostel and paying-guest options, asks seniors about commute, food and safety, and visits before paying any deposit.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: budgeting for fixed and flexible costs [Thinking]
passage: It's Ujjwal here. I share the flat's second room with Wasim, so I saw all of it. Sunday night he sat with his notebook and a calculator, talking to himself. “Rent, food, bus pass, printouts and books. That's the fixed part. Snacks and outings, that's the part I can squeeze.” Then he added a line called just in case and said, “A little each month, so I'm never stuck.” He called home and I heard him say, “Amma, can we agree on a fixed amount on the first of every month?” He said it wasn't about mistrust; it was so he would never have to ring at midnight in a panic. I can't say if he was worried or simply organised. But when the money came on the first, he put part of it into the reserve straight away.

qa.q: What did Wasim ask his mother to agree on?
qa.a: He asked to agree on a fixed amount on the first of every month.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been feeling as he made the plan, and how sure can Ujjwal be?
qa.a: Wasim seemed organised and perhaps a little worried about running short, but Ujjwal says they cannot tell which, and the just in case line suggests caution.

qa.q: What could Wasim do if the monthly amount proves too small?
qa.a: He could review it with his parents after a month or two using his written list, since real numbers show what needs to change.

qa.q: How might Wasim's mother see the fixed monthly amount?
qa.a: Amma may feel relieved that Wasim plans ahead instead of ringing in a panic, though she may also worry about him being far away.

grounding: A student lists fixed and flexible costs, adds a small reserve and agrees a monthly amount with parents so surprises do not force a midnight call.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Action]
passage: On his first evening in the hostel corridor, Dhruv knocked on the two doors next to his and said his name. On Tuesday he joined a study group in the common room, run by Ankita, a second-year who said the maths seminar was less scary in a crowd. He saved the warden's number and his local guardian's number on the first page of his phone and on a card in his wallet. Then he set a reminder: video call with Amma and Papa every Sunday at eight. When homesickness hit on Thursday night, he had somewhere to go. He texted the study group, played cards with the boy next door, and counted three days until Sunday. It wasn't perfect, but it was bearable.

qa.q: On which day and time did Dhruv schedule the calls home?
qa.a: Dhruv set the video call with Amma and Papa for every Sunday at eight.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling on Thursday night, and what helped?
qa.a: Dhruv felt homesick, and texting the study group, playing cards with the boy next door and counting three days until Sunday helped.

qa.q: What could Dhruv add if the homesickness lingers for a couple of months?
qa.a: He could speak with the warden or a counsellor, since these outlets work best alongside trained adults when a low mood does not ease.

qa.q: How might the boy next door see Dhruv's knock?
qa.a: The boy may feel welcomed and glad to have a friendly neighbour, since a hello on the first evening makes the corridor less lonely.

grounding: A newcomer greets hostel neighbours, joins a study group, saves the warden's and a guardian's numbers and schedules calls home so homesickness has outlets.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: mental simulation of the first week [Thinking]
passage:
Reena: can't sleep. I start at the new college on Monday
Damini: what's the scary part?
Reena: everything. So I'm playing it through like a film. Alarm at 6:30, tea in the mess, walk to the bus stop by 7:15
Damini: and then?
Reena: the 41 bus, 25 mins to college. I saved the route offline. If I miss it, the next one is at 7:45, still on time. Lunch: the canteen behind the library, a senior said it's cheap. I'll keep cash for it in case the payment app is down
Damini: look at you with a plan for a missed bus
Reena: it's just tiny answers. Bus missed? Next bus. No signal? Saved map. Nobody to sit with? Book in the bag
Damini: how's the panic?
Reena: smaller. not gone, but smaller 🙂

qa.q: How long does the bus ride take, and when is the next bus if Reena misses it?
qa.a: The 41 bus takes 25 mins to college, and the next one is at 7:45.

qa.q: How does Reena feel about the first day, and how has that changed?
qa.a: Reena is anxious, since the day feels scary and sleep won't come, but the panic feels smaller after playing the day through.

qa.q: What could help Reena if the fear comes back on Sunday night?
qa.a: Reena could share the plan with Damini or a college senior, because saying it aloud makes gaps easy to spot.

qa.q: How might Damini see Reena's planning?
qa.a: Damini may feel amused and proud, since the reply look at you with a plan for a missed bus shows warmth toward such careful preparation.

grounding: A teen imagines the first morning, the bus ride, lunch and a missed bus, prepares small answers like a saved route and cash, and feels less anxious.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: expecting the new place to feel like home instantly [Pitfall]
passage:
Counsellor's note, Jahnavi, hostel wing.
Sarthak arrived in July saying he would have a hundred friends by Friday. In the third week he sat in my office and said everyone else already belonged, that he was the only lonely one, and that he wanted to go home and drop out. I asked what he had expected, and he said, “I thought it would feel like home in a few days.” I told him that adjusting to a new place usually takes months, and that feeling lonely in week three is common, not a verdict on him. We wrote one small thing for each day: sit at a different mess table, say hello to one person, walk to the library with the floor. He agreed to see me on Friday and to tell his parents how he feels, without deciding anything about leaving yet. I will check in weekly.

qa.q: In which week did Sarthak say he wanted to drop out?
qa.a: In the third week, Sarthak said he wanted to go home and drop out.

qa.q: What was Sarthak feeling when he sat in the counsellor's office?
qa.a: Sarthak felt panicked and lonely, thinking everyone else already belonged and that he was the only lonely one.

qa.q: What different way of thinking could help Sarthak, and why?
qa.a: Expecting adjustment to take months and taking one small social step each day, because it makes the loneliness a normal phase rather than proof that he does not fit.

qa.q: How might Sarthak's parents feel when he tells them how he feels?
qa.a: They may feel worried and want to help, but hearing it plainly lets them support him without rushing a decision about leaving.

grounding: A student assumes he will fit in within days, feels panicked and lonely by week three and wants to drop out, not knowing adjustment takes months.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: isolating in the room and only calling home [Pitfall]
passage: The dinner bell rang at eight in the small-town hostel, and Manjula stayed in her room with the door closed. The mess was too noisy, she told herself, and the girls on her floor laughed loudly in a language she only half followed. So each evening she sat on her bed with her phone and talked to Arnab and the others from her old school, telling the same jokes for an hour. On Sunday the floor went to the temple fair together; Manjula said she had a headache. Her old friends were soon busy with their own lives, and the calls got shorter. By November she knew nobody's parents, no shop where the tea was good, and no one to sit with in the library. The town still felt like a place she was only passing through.

qa.q: What did Manjula do when the dinner bell rang each evening?
qa.a: Manjula stayed in her room with the door closed.

qa.q: Why might Manjula have said she had a headache on Sunday?
qa.a: She may feel shy and out of place among the girls and prefer the comfort of old friends, so she avoids the outing.

qa.q: What small step could help Manjula build local bonds?
qa.a: She could accept one invitation, such as tea with a girl from her floor, since small shared moments build the ties that make a town feel like home.

qa.q: How might the girls on Manjula's floor see her staying in?
qa.a: They may think she is uninterested or unfriendly, though they cannot know how uneasy she feels, so a simple invitation could open things up.

grounding: A teen avoids the mess and other students, spends evenings on the phone with old friends and misses the chance to form local bonds.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: leaning on new friends without checking their advice [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Mohit. In my second week in the city, my senior Rafiq told me about a coaching centre near the station: cheap fees, small batches, results guaranteed. “Trust me, bhai, everyone from our floor goes.” I was new and didn't want to look stupid, so I paid the whole term's fees in cash, told myself Papa would approve, and didn't ask him. I never looked at the registration or asked anyone else. Six weeks later I reached the door and found a lock and a torn notice. The fees were gone. Rafiq was as shocked as I was. Looking back, the mistake wasn't trusting a friend; it was skipping the two easy checks, asking my parents and finding out whether the centre was registered.

qa.q: What did Mohit find at the coaching centre six weeks later?
qa.a: Mohit found a lock and a torn notice.

qa.q: Why did Mohit pay the fees in cash without asking anyone?
qa.a: Mohit was new and afraid of looking stupid, so the wish to fit in mattered more than checking.

qa.q: What could Mohit do before paying for a course next time?
qa.a: Mohit could ask his parents and find out whether the centre is registered, since these two easy checks expose a doubtful offer.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when the centre closed?
qa.a: Rafiq was as shocked as Mohit, so probably embarrassed and sorry that the tip led to a loss.

grounding: A newcomer follows a senior's tip for a cheap unregistered coaching centre without asking parents or checking, and loses the fees when it closes.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: adapting routines after early problems [Revision]
passage: I'm Baljeet, and my first month in the new city ran on chai and panic. I slept late, skipped breakfast, and by eleven the words in my notes swam. My marks on the first test showed it. One evening my roommate Sunaina said, “You look like a phone on two percent.” That stung, and it was true. So I changed three things. First, a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, written on the wall. Second, a tiffin service two lanes away that brings dal and rice at one and at eight. Third, I moved my study block to five in the morning, when the hostel is quiet, instead of the noisy evenings. It took two weeks to feel normal. By the second test I could finish a chapter without my eyes closing.

qa.q: What three changes did Baljeet make?
qa.a: Baljeet set a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, found a tiffin service two lanes away, and moved the study block to five in the morning.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel when Sunaina said the remark about a phone on two percent?
qa.a: It stung, so Baljeet felt hurt, but Baljeet also knew it was true.

qa.q: What else could help if the new schedule still leaves Baljeet drained?
qa.a: Baljeet could talk to the warden, and if it keeps going or worries Baljeet, check with the doctor, since routine changes may not solve everything.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen the change?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt relieved to see Baljeet finishing chapters, since the remark came from worry as much as from teasing.

grounding: After skipping breakfast and struggling to focus, a student sets a fixed schedule, finds a nearby tiffin service and shifts study time to when the hostel is quiet.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: asking for help when homesickness lingers [Revision]
passage: Two months in, I stopped being able to sleep. I lay awake till three, then dragged myself to class with a heavy head, and I stopped laughing at anything. I told myself it was just homesickness and kept quiet. Then Alka ma'am, our warden, asked, “Beti, when did you last eat properly with someone?” and I cried in her office. She listened and took me to the college counsellor the next morning. They didn't hand me a magic fix. They asked questions and we made a plan: talk once a week, join the Saturday photography club, and a trip back home when term ends. The club was awkward at first. I'm Kavitha, and I'm sleeping a bit better now, and I know the ticket home is booked.

qa.q: Which club did Kavitha join?
qa.a: Kavitha joined the Saturday photography club.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling in the warden's office?
qa.a: Kavitha felt overwhelmed and sad, since she cried when the warden asked a caring question after weeks of keeping quiet.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do if she still feels low after the term break?
qa.a: She could keep meeting the counsellor and tell the warden or her family, since a low mood that keeps going is something to keep sharing with support.

qa.q: How might the warden see Kavitha coming in?
qa.a: Alka ma'am probably felt concerned and glad that Kavitha opened up, since she asked a caring question and acted the next morning.

grounding: After two months of poor sleep and low mood, a teen speaks to the warden and a counsellor, joins a weekend club and plans a visit home.
